findings.title: The denial cache key is ambiguous when names contain '_'.
findings.body: The key joins `name` and `parent` with '_', and dashboard and folder UIDs can contain underscores. So name=`a_b`, parent=`c` and name=`a`, parent=`b_c` produce the same key. A denial cached for one resource then denies a different resource the user can access, for the cache TTL. Fix: use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs, or encode the parts. Adding a distinct prefix also keeps these keys apart from `userPermCacheKey` in the shared cache.

findings.title: The denial cache key leaves out the identity type, so a denial can carry over to a different kind of caller.
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from namespace, `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name and folder. It does not include `checkReq.IdentityType`. Anonymous, render-service, user and service-account subjects all share the same key space. If two subjects of different types end up with the same `UserUID`, a denial cached for one is returned to the other. Two cases: anonymous and renderer subjects whose UID is empty or `0`, or a service account whose UID matches a user's. For example, after anonymous is denied dashboard X, the renderer, which normally gets fixed permissions from `getRendererPermissions`, is denied X until the TTL runs out. I could not see how `validateCheckRequest` fills `UserUID` for anonymous and renderer subjects, so check that. The fix is to add the identity type to the denial key, or to skip the denial cache for anonymous and renderer subjects.

findings.title: A cached denial blocks access to a resource that is created or granted after the denial.
findings.body: A denial is stored per (user, action, name, parent) for `shortCacheTTL`, and nothing clears it when permissions change. The denial cache is read before the permission cache and before the DB. The apiserver runs authz before storage lookup, so a check on a name that does not exist yet will be denied and cached. Examples: a GET on a dashboard UID before it is imported or provisioned, or a check before the creator's permission row is written. Then the creator is refused for the full TTL even though the DB now grants access. That is the exact problem this PR is meant to fix. Granting a user access to a resource they were just denied has the same delay. Fix: give denials a much shorter TTL, or delete or bypass matching denial entries when resource permissions are written.

findings.title: The denial-cache test seeds a deny, so it would pass without the denial cache.
findings.body: The comment says the permission cache grants access, to show the denial cache wins. But the map value is `false`, so `checkPermission` denies anyway. The DB fallback (an empty fakeStore) also denies. The test would pass even if the denial cache were never read. Set the value to `true` so the test actually checks that the denial short-circuits.
